# Why Modern Four-Stroke Engines Use Wasted Spark Systems

In a typical inline-four or V6 engine, ignition coils fire in pairs. When cylinder one is on its power stroke, firing the spark plug, cylinder four is simultaneously at Top Dead Center (TDC) during its exhaust stroke. The system fires both plugs at once: the active cylinder ignites the air-fuel mixture for combustion, while the inactive cylinder experiences a "wasted spark" against its open intake or exhaust valves.

You might wonder why manufacturers don't simply use individual coils for every cylinder to eliminate this inefficiency. While it is true that dedicated coils would prevent wasting energy on non-compression strokes and theoretically reduce plug wear by halving the frequency of firing, the engineering reality involves more than just component longevity. The decision to stick with wasted spark systems often hinges on a balance between electrical complexity, packaging constraints, and cost-effectiveness that goes beyond simple unit pricing.

## Electrical Load and Alternator Sizing

The primary technical reason for avoiding individual coils lies in the electrical architecture of the vehicle. Ignition coils are essentially step-up transformers that convert low-voltage battery power (12V) into high voltage (20,000V+) required to jump the spark plug gap. This process draws a significant amount of current from the alternator.

In a wasted spark system with two cylinders per coil, the electrical load is halved compared to a dedicated coil-per-cylinder setup. If you were to equip an engine with individual coils, the peak current draw during ignition events would increase substantially. While modern alternators are robust, increasing their capacity requires larger pulleys and physically bigger units that must be mounted in tight under-hood spaces. For manufacturers designing for global markets where vehicle size is often constrained by regulations or market expectations, keeping the alternator smaller saves weight and packaging volume.

## Packaging and Reliability Trade-offs

The user's concern about space is valid; a bank of individual coils does require more physical volume than a single coil pack covering two cylinders. However, the argument for wasted spark isn't just about fitting components under the hood—it's also about reliability and thermal management.

Dedicated coil-on-plug (COP) systems place an ignition module directly on or inside each spark plug boot. This arrangement simplifies the wiring harness but introduces a point of failure for every single cylinder. If you have eight cylinders, you now have eight distinct high-voltage connections and eight potential failure points in the ignition electronics. A wasted spark system reduces this count by half. Furthermore, consolidating coils allows heat to be dissipated more effectively through larger metal housings rather than isolated small modules that might overheat during consecutive firing events.

It is also worth noting that while dedicated coils eliminate the wasted spark on the inactive plug, they do not necessarily reduce wear on the active plug compared to a well-tuned wasted spark system. The energy delivered in both cases must still overcome the gap resistance and initiate combustion. In fact, some studies suggest that the "wasted" portion of the spark can actually help clean carbon deposits from the insulator, though this effect is marginal compared to the benefits of a fresh air-fuel mixture.

## Two-Cylinder and Odd-Number Engines

Regarding your bonus questions on smaller engine configurations: two-cylinder engines almost universally utilize wasted spark systems. The firing order in an inline-two typically fires cylinders 1 and 2 simultaneously, with one always on compression and the other on exhaust or intake. Separating them would require a complex dual-coil setup that offers negligible benefit given the low displacement of each cylinder.

As for odd-numbered engines like straight-sixes or V-fives, they do not suffer from wasted spark issues in the same way. In a six-cylinder engine with a firing order of 1-5-3-6-2-4, no two cylinders are ever at TDC simultaneously during their compression strokes. Each cylinder has its own unique ignition timing point, allowing for individual coils without any wasted sparks. This is why inline-sixes often feature coil-on-plug setups as standard equipment; the packaging challenge of fitting six separate coils into a long engine block is manageable because there is no technical penalty for doing so.

## When Dedicated Coils Become Necessary

Despite the prevalence of wasted spark systems, many modern vehicles—especially high-performance or luxury models—are shifting toward individual coils. This shift isn't driven by fear of plug wear but by the need for precise control over ignition timing and energy delivery. Individual coils allow the Engine Control Unit (ECU) to adjust the dwell time and voltage independently for each cylinder, optimizing performance across a wider RPM range.

If you are building a custom vehicle or modifying an engine for track use, switching to individual coils might make sense if your alternator can handle the increased load and if your engine bay has the clearance. However, for standard production vehicles, the wasted spark system remains the most efficient compromise between cost, weight, packaging, and reliability. It is a classic example of engineering pragmatism: solving enough problems while avoiding the creation of new ones that outweigh the benefits.
